title: When the saints go marching in
word: When the saints go marching in
hookLine: spirituals turned Revelation into hope: wanting to be in that number

lines: A BRASS BAND ON THE STREET.
cards: A brass band starts up on a street. A trombone slides, a drum kicks in, and people who were only watching fall in behind.
The tune is When the Saints Go Marching In, sung slow in churches and played fast by bands, and nobody can say for certain who first sang it.
Under the bounce there's one plain wish: when the saints go marching in on the last day, the singer wants to be in that number. Counted. Not watching from the curb.
Some listeners hear that number in the seventh chapter of Revelation.

teach.b: First, the number John hears: "And I heard the number of them which were sealed: and there were sealed an hundred and forty and four thousand of all the tribes of the children of Israel." A precise count, tribe by tribe.

teach.h: A MULTITUDE NO MAN COULD NUMBER.
teach.b: Second, what John sees when he looks up: "After this I beheld, and, lo, a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands."
He hears a number, then sees a crowd nobody can count. Christians explain the two as two groups, or as one people seen two ways. Third, who they are.
An elder tells John: "These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb." People who came through hard things.
And the chapter ends with a line this block has met before: "God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes." Fourth, who counts as a saint.
In Paul's letters the word means a church's members: "to all the saints in Christ Jesus which are at Philippi."
Catholic and Orthodox Christians, and some Protestants, also honor particular saints by name, with feast days; other Protestants keep the word mostly for the whole church.

Either way, the song isn't about a few well-known names. Other spirituals sing Bible pictures as present hope too: a chariot swinging low, a balm in Gilead. This one puts the singer in the crowd before the throne.

how: When the Saints Go Marching In is sung in some churches and played by brass bands, including at funerals in New Orleans, and some churches read Revelation 7:9–17 on All Saints' Day.

games.q: what does “when the saints go marching in” mean?
o: a song with one wish: to be counted among the saints
a hymn sung only as the coffin enters the church
a marching song soldiers sang heading into battle

p: counted from the tribes of Israel
washed in the blood of the Lamb

s: in Paul's letters, saints means only a few well-known holy people
he writes "to all the saints in Christ Jesus which are at Philippi."
the multitude in Revelation 7 comes from all nations and tongues
"of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues."
Revelation 7 ends with God wiping away tears
"God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes."

games.q: you're John. you've just heard the number of the sealed, tribe by tribe. then you look up. what do you see?
o: exactly that many people, standing in rows.
a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations.
games.why: "lo, a great multitude, which no man could number." a number heard, then a crowd too big to count.

practice: Sing or hum the song softly and slowly, more hymn than parade, or hum any tune you love if you don't know it.

Between the lines, bring to mind the people you'd want in that number with you, someone who taught you, someone who came through something hard, someone you've lost, and let the crowd grow past what you can count.
If you pray, hold them before God; if not, just sing them in.

wordCard.voice: When the saints go marching in. A song with one wish, to be counted among the saints, and, some hear, Revelation's multitude which no man could number.

orig.note: Greek: a great crowd, a multitude. Revelation 7:9.

carryVoice: Your line: in that number. A number no one could count. Rest well.
